The name of the offering is disputed before anything else is settled. Calvin rejects the usual rendering as unsuitable and the alternative that makes them sacrifices of perfections as far-fetched, and since the Hebrew word for peace takes in safety and all good success he prefers to render the plural as prosperities, noting that David calls the libation used in this sacrifice the cup of salvations. Gill reports the Targums calling them sacrifices of holinesses, and is careful that this does not mean they were holier than others, since they ranked among the lighter holy things; the Greek version calls them sacrifices of salvation, and one Jewish commentator derives the name from their bringing peace between God and men. Clarke takes it simply as an offering to make peace between God and man. Henry keeps both senses at once. Peace means reconciliation and communion, so that God and his people feast together in token of friendship, the priest acting as the days-man who lays his hand on both, since they could not eat together unless agreed; and it means prosperity, so that the offering was brought either to ask a mercy or to acknowledge one received. Wesley makes the same division, a thank-offering when the blessing is obtained and a kind of supplication when it is desired.

Against the burnt offering the differences are set out point by point. Henry founds them on what each regards: the burnt offering has to do with God as in himself the best of beings, is purely adoration, and is therefore wholly burnt, while the peace offering has to do with God as benefactor and is accordingly divided between the altar, the priest and the owner. Wesley repeats that distinction almost word for word, and adds a consequence of his own: a female was allowed here though not there because the burnt offering principally respects the honour of God, who is to be served with the best, while this one respects the benefit of the offerer, so the choice was left to him. Ellicott confirms the point from the law itself, that no distinction of sex is made and no limit of age, only that the animal be free of organic defect. He also notes that the hand laid on the head here carried no confession of sin but words of praise, which Gill has as well on the authority of Maimonides. Keil supplies the reason pigeons were excluded, that a sacrificial meal always accompanied this offering and a pair of birds would not suffice for one.

The fat is where the anatomists take over. Ellicott explains why it is specified at all, that the word means the best or choicest part, used elsewhere of the finest produce of the ground, and that being most valuable it belonged to God and so acquired a sanctity which forbade its being eaten. Keil identifies each portion in turn: the large net that stretches from the stomach over the bowels and abounds with fat in ruminants, the fat attached to the intestines which could easily be peeled off, the two kidneys with the fat about them in the region of the loins, and the net upon the liver. Clarke names the same parts by their Latin terms, the omentum or caul and the mesentery that connects the convolutions of the intestines. Keil then refuses a proposed rendering, that the fat was burnt in the manner of the burnt offering, holding that the preposition will not bear it and that the daily offering was already alight, so the pieces were laid on top of it. Gill reads the burning as signifying the sufferings by which peace was made, and the kidneys as the flaming affections of Christ. Calvin answers the objection that such minuteness about trifles is superfluous, since the exactness itself taught that something higher was wrapped in the ceremonies.
6:
Henry begins by explaining an absence. Turtle-doves and young pigeons, admissible for whole burnt offerings, are not allowed here, because they carry no fat considerable enough to burn upon the altar and would come to next to nothing once divided according to the law of this offering. Beyond that he finds the rules for a lamb or a goat much the same as for a bullock. On the animal itself Ellicott and Gill differ over a word. Ellicott holds that what the English renders a lamb is better given as a sheep, since the term denotes a full-grown animal and is so rendered elsewhere; Gill cites a rule of Maimonides that wherever the word occurs in the law it means one of the first year. Ellicott adds that sheep and goats alike might be male or female provided they were without organic defect, and Gill notes the Targum's addition that the hand laid on the head was the right hand, laid with strength.

The fat tail draws three separate excursions into natural history, each resting on a different authority. Ellicott identifies the broad-tailed species of Syria and Palestine, the broad part often weighing fifteen pounds and upwards, its substance between marrow and fat, tasting like marrow in young animals and used by the Arabs for cooking in place of butter; it grows so large that a small wheeled truck is fastened under it to spare the animal the pain of dragging it. Keil reports the same practice from his own sources, adding that such sheep are found in Northern Africa, Egypt, Arabia and Syria, and that while ordinary sheep occur elsewhere, in modern Palestine the whole stock is of the broad-tailed kind. Clarke draws on a physician's account of the sheep at Aleppo, where the tails are not eaten separately but mixed with the lean meat or used instead of butter, and gives the weights: a common carcass sixty to seventy pounds with a tail of fifteen, and the largest breed a hundred and fifty with tails of fifty. Ellicott adds the ritual consequence, that this tail alone among fats is offered yet is not reckoned ordinary fat, so by Jewish tradition it escapes the prohibition. Henry takes the moral instead, that a thing however contemptible can be made honourable by being applied to God's service.

Calling the burnt portion the food of the offering is treated as a deliberate figure. Ellicott takes it as the bread which the altar fire was to consume for God, and points out that what was burnt is elsewhere called his bread, the priests being described as offering the bread of their God. Wesley reads it as the fuel of the fire, or the matter of the offering, and says it is called bread to mark God's acceptance of it and his delight in it, as men delight in their food. Clarke presses the image further, that God is frequently represented as feasting with his people on their sacrifices, and since these were consumed by fire kindled from heaven they were reckoned the food of that fire, or rather of the Being it represented; he notes on another's authority that in the same idiom the gods of the heathen are said to eat the fat and drink the wine consumed on their altars. Henry keeps the domestic sense, that in the tabernacle God was keeping house among them, and by the offerings on the altar kept a good table. Gill observes what the goat's ritual lacks by comparison, that nothing is said of the fat of the rump and tail as it was for the lamb.

Ellicott ties the two verses together as one argument: the pieces are burnt because they constitute the bread of Jehovah, and it is precisely because the fat belongs to the Lord that its eating is forbidden for ever. Gill fills in what was actually burnt, which was not the fat only but the inwards and the kidneys with it, and reports from Maimonides that the priest salted the parts before laying them on the altar, and that the breast and shoulder due to the priests could not be taken until the burning was done. Wesley notices an omission by comparison with the sheep, that the tail is not among the parts here, since in goats it is a refuse part. Calvin explains why these duties fall to the priest at all, sprinkling the blood and casting the fat into the fire, on the ground that he alone was competent to make atonement.

The word food gives Calvin his opening and also his difficulty. He grants the metaphor is harsh and defends it as admirably expressing what is meant, that the legal service pleased God as the food we eat pleases us, and that it marks a familiar communion, as though he sat at the same table with his people. God, who breathes life into all and borrows nothing, plainly does not want food; but his kindness could not be better shown than by deigning to become the messmate of his worshippers, and the prophet's reproach that the table of the Lord is polluted turns on that same figure, the offence being not that God delighted in fat but that so extraordinary a pledge of grace was neglected. The similitude must then be carried back to what it represents, that the exercise of faith is as pleasing to him as a sumptuous feast. Having said that, Calvin admits he cannot see clearly why God claims the fat in all the sacrifices and orders it burnt, unless it was to accustom his servants to temperance, the fat being reckoned the choicest part.

How far the prohibition reaches is the chapter's last question, and the answers narrow it in different ways. Clarke argues from butchery that fat cannot be forbidden as absolutely as blood: blood is contained in separate vessels and can be entirely drained by cutting the throat, which was the Jewish method, whereas fat is intimately intermixed with the muscular fibres and cannot be separated. So what is meant must be fat in a separate state, the caul, the fat of the mesentery, the fat on the kidneys and the whole of the tail, and probably only in animals offered in sacrifice. Wesley limits it the same two ways, to beasts sacrificed or fit to be sacrificed and to fat easily separable, allowing that what runs through the flesh might be eaten. Gill reports the contrary opinion, that Jewish writers take the law generally, since sacrifices were not offered in private dwellings, while a Targum's addition seems to restrain it to sacrifice after all. Wesley supplies three grounds for the rule, reverence for the rites, acknowledgment that God may reserve what he pleases of his own creatures, and the exercise of self-denial in a thing many would much desire. Ellicott ends on the wording, that the full legislative formula occurs only four times in the Pentateuch and should be rendered alike in all four.
